items.source: A power chord plays only the root and the fifth, the note five letters up. Neither major nor minor, it stays punchy, even loud. E5 is the bottom of E minor.
items.note: Source describes a fifth as five letters up/above. A literal reader might count five transitions rather than five names including both endpoints. Hebrew is faithful; later theory explicitly counts both ends. Optional source-owner clarification, not a target defect.

items.source: B7 is five letters up from E. Five letters up from A is E, so E7 takes its place.

items.source: E, D, C: three steps down to home.
items.note: Source calls E, D, C three steps down although it contains two adjacent transitions. Target retains the source shorthand; optional source-owner precision.

items.source: Open B, D at fret 3, open E and back. Then G and G sharp on string 3, sliding into open B.
items.note: Source slide wording approaches open B from G/G-sharp on string 3. Hebrew frames smooth approach rather than requiring a literal fretted slide across strings; musical intent is preserved.

items.source: A sharp sits between A and B, at fret 3 on string 3. It slides up into open B, the bluesy lift that gives gospel its sound.
items.note: Source A-sharp on string 3 slides into open B. Target keeps the pitch-motion metaphor; an actual one-finger slide to a different open string is not mechanically literal. Source-owner technique wording may be clarified.

items.source: From A, put finger 4 on string 2, fret 3 for Asus4. Lift the finger off string 2 and let it ring open for Asus2. Both fall back to A.
items.note: Source lift-finger transition from Asus4 toward Asus2 can depend on which underlying fingers remain down. Target preserves source instruction; source fingering demonstration may merit checking.
